rv.q: Happily, nothing as catty can be said of the rest of this fabulous revival of the 1981 musical phenom that padded its way around the world on little cats' feet.

And so “Cats” remains precisely what it always was, a tuneful ball of coiled dancers’ energy and the useful vehicle for a discovery of the wonder of musical theater, most especially when a wide-eyed seven-year-old is in tow.
As for the latter, this slightly scaled-down and rejiggered version is unlikely to change their minds.
Note to Ms. Lynne: Mild battery would really be sufficient.
The performances, though, are uneven.
They held my attention when nothing else did, which was usually.
For the resistant rest of us, alas, “Cats” remains an overblown kiddie show.
Too slow, too tame, too threadbare.
Yet such is the innate confidence and innocent zest of this bizarre, feline spectacle that all cynicism just moults away.
The wan revival that opens tonight at the Neil Simon at least gets the lighting (by Natasha Katz) right.
Cats is an attenuated high-concept revue that grows tedious by its second act.
So it was an extraordinary surprise that the Cats revival at the Theatre turned out to be a melodious, witty and—most shocking!—worthwhile, stylish entertainment.

"No doubt the success of the 2014 revival of 'Cats' in London encouraged the producers to bring it back to New York. And wisely, they've done so with a new cast of top to bottom standouts and vital and fresh choreography that retained the feeling of the original. This does indeed boost the show's strong points...

But this production proves, despite its missteps, that it's capable of harnessing pure theatrical enjoyment for two and a half hours, and conjure an experience more memorable than many of today's overworked and overworkshopped offerings.

“For those who saw the original mega-hit, things look strikingly familiar...Where this ‘Cats’ strays from its predecessor is in its choreography, brilliantly reimagined by Andy Blankenbuehler and based on original choreography by Gillian Lynne...Leona Lewis' performance is a weak link in an otherwise stellar ensemble of triple-threats...
A newcomer to the show watching the sweet and endearing revival now gracing the Theatre may find it surprising to know how polarizing Cats was during its original 18-year stay.
This new 'Cats' is peppy and kinetic, if sometimes a tad monotonous.
It's hard to escape the feeling that a very casual piece of source material has been blown up far beyond its limits into something only intermittently charming-and often perplexing.
And after a bit, all these impeccably costumed folks begin to blend together in a tabby tuffet that becomes too much of a good thing.
But my biggest criticism is the key role of Grizabella.
If you know Cats, this is essentially the Cats you know and either love or hate.
This revival provokes but one response to the show’s onetime tagline: now and whatever.
Plotless, repetitive, nonsensical, the '80s relic quickly turns tiresome enough to make you wish for a catnap.
So when someone tries to tell you that Cats is old fashioned or too campy for its own good, prove to them how the show is now a classic that was ahead of its time.
It’s as fresh and lively as if it had been newly created.
This is above all a spectacle with appeal to those who get theatergoing kicks from costumes, lighting, cast members roaming the aisles to sing to spectators, and assorted scenic stunts.
I still can't say Cats is my favorite musical ever—far from it—but I enjoyed this revival at the Theatre.
Your inner theater snob may tell you it's too silly a spectacle to bother with, but your outer theater geek will fight for the right to enjoy it.
That said, the named Cats and the Cats chorus provides sufficient energy to overcome this significant flaw in the current production.
It is also hands-down the most openly bizarre piece of entertainment to ever be so popular.
Every otherwise humdrum minute of this show is the cat’s meow because of her varied and skilled use of lighting.
Now it all just seems too familiar.
Cats is an entertainment, made of song and dance, both of which it’s got covered in spades.

“One wonders if Mr. Nunn’s revival might have been more powerful had he put a modern, fresh spin on the show...However, gimmicky revivals almost never work so Mr. Nunn was wise not to tamper too much with Mr. Lloyd Webber’s winning formula.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this nostalgic revival, praising the energetic cast and spectacular dancing while questioning the plotless material's staying power. It divides audiences into devoted fans and bewildered skeptics, just as it did in 1982.

vs.sum: The Neil Simon Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although comfort is compromised by tight legroom and narrow seats. The ambiance is appealing with its classic architectural charm, and facilities are average, with typical restroom and concession offerings.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Step-free from street to Orchestra. No elevator.
